title: Choosing Among Discrete Values with switch

blocks.text: Selecting by equality

When a decision compares the same category against several constant values, switch can express that selection directly. In these first examples, the category has type int or char. A case marks the point where control transfers when its value matches; default handles values that match no case. Do not use switch for ranges, conditions with &&, or std::string strings: keep if for those rules (Stroustrup, 2024, sections 3.4.1.2–3.4.1.3).

With opcion equal to 2, execution enters case 2 and prints Show. break ends the switch. The program continues after its closing brace. Labels are not if questions evaluated one after another: first the entry point is selected, and then execution follows the statements reachable from it.

blocks.text: Labels do not stop execution

If execution reaches the end of a case's statements without break or another transfer of control, it continues into the statements that follow, even if they are under another label. This is called fallthrough. The category's value does not change when execution passes another label. For mutually exclusive alternatives, explicitly leave the switch after each action (Stroustrup, 2024, section 3.4.1.3).

blocks.text: Group labels and select characters

You can place several consecutive labels before the same action to explicitly share a response. Each case uses a constant value, and two cases in the same switch cannot have the same value. For char, use single quotes around character literals; "g" would be a different, string literal. Do not rely on any particular numeric encoding of characters.

blocks.explanation: Each selected value must identify an entry point without duplicate labels.

blocks.text: A switch inside a loop

break exits the innermost loop or switch that contains it. If a switch is inside a for loop and break is inside the switch, that break ends the switch; it does not end the surrounding for loop. Read this rule through the nesting, not visual alignment (Working draft: Programming languages — C++, n.d., section [stmt.break]).

When continuing into the next case is intentional

In the previous selector, the actions were exclusive: removing break broke the rule. Now consider a different rule. Command 1 must prepare and then review; command 2 must review directly. We can put the review in the second case and let the first reach it after preparing. That fallthrough is intentional because it represents two stages required by the problem. It does not turn command 1 into command 2.

Write [[fallthrough]]; to indicate that the continuation is intentional. It is an attribute, an annotation that communicates our intention to the compiler (Stroustrup, 2024, section 3.4.1.3). Here it accompanies a null statement, so it ends with a semicolon. It performs no operation and does not jump to another label; execution continues because there is no break to stop it. In this simple use, it is placed after the first case's last action and before the next case or default of the same switch (Working draft: Programming languages — C++, n.d., section [dcl.attr.fallthrough]).

With orden equal to 1, the program displays Prepare;Review;End. Initial selection enters case 1. Execution then reaches the review, even though the case 2 label does not match value 1. The break at the second stage does end the switch. With orden equal to 2, execution enters the review directly without preparing. This differs from grouping two empty labels: here the first entry performs an additional action before sharing the second stage.

blocks.question: Predict the entire output. Also observe orden after the switch: falling through does not change its value.
blocks.explanation: The program prepares from case 1 and reaches the review in case 2. No statement assigns a new value to orden, which remains 1. A label marks an entry point, not a new comparison that prevents execution from continuing.

blocks.text: Choose according to the requirement: break to end an alternative; [[fallthrough]]; to document an intended continuation. Adding the attribute to accidental fallthrough does not fix the behavior. The compiler may warn about fallthrough without this annotation; the absence of a warning does not prove that the program follows the problem's rule.
Express the intention in the right place

blocks.question: Command 1 must prepare and review; command 2 must only review. Fill in just the attribute that declares the fallthrough intentional. The semicolon is already supplied.
blocks.explanation: [[fallthrough]]; declares the intended continuation between the two stages. break would prevent reviewing after preparing. The annotation uses two opening and two closing square brackets.

blocks.question: In these directly executed cases, where should you write [[fallthrough]]; to continue from preparing to reviewing?
options: After preparing, immediately before the review case in the same switch.
After the closing brace of the switch, before printing End.
At the end of the last case, even if only the closing brace of the switch follows.
Before the statement printing Prepare, without the attribute's semicolon.
blocks.explanation: The attribute annotates a null statement, and the next statement to execute must have a case or default label in the same switch. It does not apply to the Prepare output and cannot be used outside the switch. The annotation is invalid without a later case to continue into.

blocks.text: Build a shared stage with a summary

A station repeats the same command repeticiones times, from 0 to 4. Command 1 performs one preparation and one review per iteration. Command 2 performs only a review. Any other integer orden counts as unknown, without preparing or reviewing. The data are already set in the code; you do not need to read input. Before programming, calculate the numbers of preparations, reviews, and unknown commands for (orden,repeticiones) equal to (1,3), (2,3), (9,3), and (1,0).

Build the loop and all three counters from this minimal editor. Use a switch on each iteration: in case 1, perform the preparation and declare fallthrough with [[fallthrough]]; the review must appear only once, in case 2. End that stage and the unknown alternative with break. Print just one summary after the loop, in the exact format Preparations=3;Reviews=3;Unknown=0 for the initial case. Decide where to declare each object so the summary retains results from all iterations.

Check the three rules separately, as well as the zero-iteration case. With command 2 and three repetitions, the summary must show zero preparations, three reviews, and zero unknown commands. With command 9 and three repetitions: zero, zero, and three. With zero repetitions, all three counters must remain zero for any command. Also test one and four repetitions, as well as commands -1 and 0. Keep your attempt before consulting the reference. The lab does not automatically grade the program: compare its output against the requirements and explain the first difference.
Compare the shared stage and recall its purpose

Consult this implementation after building and checking your attempt. The counters are initialized only once before the loop. The first stage adds one preparation and continues to the only review statement. Command 2 enters that review directly; default preserves a separate reason in the third counter.

For (1,3), (2,3), (9,3), and (1,0), the three totals are respectively (3,3,0), (0,3,0), (0,0,3), and (0,0,0). With one repetition, command 1 contributes (1,1,0); with four, it contributes (4,4,0). Any other command, including -1 and 0, increases only the unknown count. A break after preparation would lose the reviews for command 1. Reinitializing counters inside the loop would lose previous iterations. The repeticiones range is part of the requirement; this reference does not validate external data.

blocks.question: You remove only the [[fallthrough]]; line from the reference, leaving all other statements unchanged. What changes when orden is 1?
options: The program still prepares and reviews; only the explicit annotation of that intention is lost.
The review no longer happens because the attribute was the instruction that jumped to case 2.
orden changes to 2, so only review happens from then on.
blocks.explanation: Fallthrough happens because execution continues without break. The attribute documents that intention and may affect compiler warnings, but changes neither execution nor orden. To make an exclusive alternative, you would need to change the control flow with break and verify whether that matches the desired rule.

blocks.question: Now the commands change between iterations: 1, 2, and 3. Predict the summary before running the program; explain which command contributes to each counter.
blocks.explanation: Command 1 prepares and reviews; command 2 only reviews; command 3 only increases the unknown count. Each break ends the switch and allows the next iteration. Sharing the stage does not require every iteration to begin at the same label.

blocks.text: The book distinguishes accidental fallthrough from explicitly intended fallthrough using [[fallthrough]]; (Stroustrup, 2024, section 3.4.1.3). To clarify its placement and semicolon, we also consulted section [dcl.attr.fallthrough] of the public working draft (Working draft: Programming languages — C++, n.d.).
